Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette: Eleanor Vance still remembers the heavy oak door slamming shut behind them, a sound that instantly locked her joints. She had met him through a known acquaintance, a friend turned lover, which made his violence feel like a betrayal of reality itself. When he struck her, it was always in that narrow hallway, his familiar face contorted. Now, at eighty, the mere sight of a man standing too close in her social work office, leaning over a case file, instantly pulls up fragmented moments of that hallway, each stuck in her mind like a photograph, unable to be placed in sequence. The intrusion of those disjointed snapshots immediately deepened her conviction that the world’s foundational rules had been obliterated, leaving her certain that people could not be trusted. She had come to believe that male presence and known faces were simply masks waiting to slip, and this sudden fear of a familiar person would immediately trigger a fresh wave of panic. To manage the rising panic, she began scanning every room and building for the nearest exit, her eyes darting to windows and fire doors before she even hung her coat. Her hypervigilance and chronic sleep problems meant she could not rest, so she adopted the habit of avoiding dreams by deliberately staying awake past midnight, sipping tea and reviewing old case files. Because she felt perpetually contaminated by the memory of his hands, she started actively erasing the memory of the event whenever it surfaced, forcing herself to look away from photographs or change the subject when colleagues mentioned domestic violence. The intrusive force of those disjointed snapshots directly prompted her to adopt memory erasure as a defense, while her conviction that she was fundamentally contaminated and that people could not be trusted kept her threat system locked in overdrive, manifesting as relentless scanning for exits and chronic sleep problems. Her conviction that the world’s foundational rules had been obliterated drove her to adopt rigid coping rituals, specifically choosing to avoid dreams and actively erase the memory of the event whenever they surfaced. By preventing herself from processing the trauma, her active avoidance strategies ensured her threat system remained chronically activated, which meant her eyes stayed locked on the heavy oak door at the end of the corridor every time she entered a new room. Her reliance on these avoidance strategies actually amplified her triggers, ensuring that even minor cues like a slamming door or a familiar voice would bypass her filters and strike with full force. Every time a disjointed snapshot of that hallway surfaced, it would instantly reactivate her triggers, making her hyperalert to any familiar face or male presence. Her chronic threat state meant that even a mundane auditory cue like a door opening would instantly register as a signal of danger, bypassing reason and locking her into fight-or-flight. At her current outreach center, she would sit rigidly at her desk, unable to focus on client files until she had mentally mapped three possible exits. Over the decades, these habits calcified into an inescapable routine that isolated her from peers, as she declined social invitations to avoid known people and refused to let anyone sit on the side of the desk that blocked the exit. At eighty, the weight of this unbroken cycle finally broke her resolve. She walked into a community mental health clinic not for the first time, hoping a therapist might help her untangle the knot, though she remained terrified that seeking help would only force her to confront the truth that her beliefs had been destroyed and that no amount of scanning or erasure could ever make her feel clean again. She knew her avoidance strategies were keeping her trapped; by erasing the memory of the event and avoiding dreams, she had only ensured that the contamination and mistrust would fester, feeding back into her constant scanning and sleepless nights. Yet, for the first time, she brought her case files to a new intake session, hoping someone might finally help her find meaning in why the event had happened to her, rather than continuing to erase the memory of the event.
